analytics.title: From Calendar Chaos to Clinical Efficiency

overview.text: The Sleep and CPAP Center relied on Google Calendar to manage patient appointments, insurance information, and doctor referrals, resulting in scattered data, inefficient workflows, and difficulties tracking insurance claims. To address these challenges, I designed a custom ERP system tailored to the clinic’s operational needs. The solution centralized patient management, streamlined appointment scheduling, and enabled structured insurance claim tracking, improving administrative efficiency and reducing manual workload for staff. This project focused on transforming a fragmented process into an organized, scalable healthcare management system through user-centered design.

analytics.problem: "The Sleep and CPAP Center relied on Google Calendar to manage patient, referral, and insurance information, leading to fragmented data, inefficient workflows, and difficulty tracking insurance claims."

goal.title: Design a centralized ERP system to streamline patient management and insurance claim tracking.
goal.text:
• Centralize patient, referral, and insurance information in one system
  • Simplify appointment scheduling and management
  • Enable easy tracking of insurance claims
  • Improve workflow efficiency for clinic staff
  • Minimize data errors and information loss

discover.text:
User interviews revealed that administrative staff relied heavily on manual processes to manage daily operations. Google Calendar was used as a central tool, but it lacked structure for handling healthcare-specific data such as patient histories, insurance details, and referral tracking. Staff frequently switched between entries to locate information, increasing cognitive load and slowing down workflows. Insurance claim follow-ups were particularly challenging due to the absence of status tracking, leading to delays and missed updates. Users expressed a strong need for a centralized system that could simplify tasks, improve visibility, and reduce repetitive work.

Key Findings:
  • Patient information was scattered across multiple calendar entries
  • Insurance claim status was difficult to track and monitor
  • Staff spent significant time searching for and updating information
  • Manual data handling increased the risk of errors
  • No standardized workflow for managing referrals and claims
  • Users needed a centralized and structured management system
  • Visibility into daily operations and patient progress was limited

define.text:
Based on research insights, several opportunities emerged to improve the clinic’s workflow and operational efficiency:

How Might We
  • How might we centralize patient and insurance information to reduce data fragmentation?
  • How might we help staff quickly track insurance claim progress?
  • How might we simplify appointment management for administrative users?
  • How might we reduce manual work and repetitive data entry?
  • How might we improve visibility into patient and clinic operations?

Solution:
  • Create a centralized platform to manage patients, appointments, referrals, and insurance data
  • Design structured data entry to reduce errors and inconsistencies
  • Provide clear visibility into insurance claim status and progress
  • Simplify appointment scheduling with healthcare-specific workflows
  • Reduce administrative workload through intuitive navigation and automation
  • Enable quick access to patient information during daily operations
  • Support scalable workflows as the clinic grows

Information Architecture:
To support efficient workflows, the ERP system was structured around the clinic’s primary tasks and user needs. The information architecture focused on organizing data into clear, task-oriented modules.
  • Dashboard — Overview of appointments, pending claims, and daily activities
  • Patient Management — Patient profiles, medical details, referral information
  • Appointments — Scheduling, calendar view, and visit management
  • Insurance Claims — Claim creation, status tracking, and documentation
  • Referrals — Doctor referral records and follow-ups
  • Reports — Operational and claim performance insights
  • Settings — User roles and system configuration
This structure allowed users to navigate based on their workflow rather than searching through scattered information, improving efficiency and reducing cognitive load.

design.intro: The ERP system was designed through a user-centered process focused on understanding real clinic workflows and operational challenges. The project began with user interviews and workflow analysis to identify pain points in patient management and insurance tracking. Insights from research were translated into user flows and information architecture that reflected staff tasks rather than technical structures. Low-fidelity wireframes were created to explore layout and navigation, followed by iterative refinements based on usability considerations. The final design prioritized centralized information, clear workflow visibility, and action-oriented interfaces, resulting in a scalable ERP system tailored to the daily needs of the Sleep and CPAP Center.

items.text:
Design Decisions
The design of the Patient Information page was guided by research insights, workflow analysis, and the operational needs of administrative staff. Each interface decision was intentionally made to reduce complexity, improve visibility, and support real-world clinic tasks.

1. Prioritizing a Single Source of Truth
Problem: Patient, insurance, and referral data were previously scattered across multiple Google Calendar entries, forcing staff to search repeatedly for information.
Design Decision: All patient-related information was consolidated into one unified page.
Why: Creating a single workspace reduces context switching, improves confidence in data accuracy, and allows users to complete tasks without navigating across multiple tools.

2.Designing Around Workflow, Not Data Types
Problem: Users think in terms of tasks (scheduling, claims, billing), not databases or categories.
Design Decision: A workflow progress tracker was introduced at the top of the page to reflect real clinic processes.
Why: Aligning the interface with users’ mental models helps staff instantly understand patient status and prevents missed operational steps.

3. Progressive Information Organization
Problem: Displaying all patient information at once created overwhelm and slowed task completion.
Design Decision: Information was divided into task-based tabs such as Insurance Info, Billing Info, and Patient History.
Why: Progressive disclosure allows users to focus only on relevant information while maintaining easy access to supporting data.

4. Visualizing Insurance Complexity
Problem: Insurance details were difficult to interpret quickly, causing delays and frequent verification checks.
Design Decision: Insurance data was presented using structured cards separating authorization, coverage, and financial breakdowns.
Why: Visual grouping transforms complex financial information into scannable content, enabling faster decision-making during patient interactions.

5. Action-First Interface Layout
Problem: Staff frequently performed scheduling actions but previously navigated through multiple steps.
Design Decision: Primary actions (Schedule HST, In-Lab, CPAP Setup) were placed prominently within the patient overview panel.
Why: Reducing interaction steps improves efficiency and supports high-frequency tasks in busy clinical environments.

6. Reducing Cognitive Load Through Visual Hierarchy
Problem: Users struggled to identify important information quickly.
Design Decision: Clear hierarchy was created using card layouts, spacing, and grouped sections.
Why: A scannable interface allows users to locate information within seconds, which is critical in operational healthcare workflows.

7. Supporting Error Prevention
Problem: Manual entry and unstructured notes increased mistakes.
Design Decision: Structured fields and standardized layouts replaced free-form data storage.
Why: Consistent patterns reduce ambiguity and minimize operational errors.

Workflow Status Bar Design
The status bar was designed to give administrative staff a clear, real time understanding of a patient’s progress throughout the treatment, billing, and insurance workflow. During research, users highlighted difficulty tracking patient stages when information was stored in calendar notes, often leading to missed follow-ups and delayed insurance actions. The status bar addresses this by transforming complex operational steps into a visual, easy-to-scan workflow.

1. Making Patient Progress Visible
Problem: Staff struggled to understand where a patient was in the treatment and insurance process because progress was previously tracked through scattered calendar notes and manual updates.
Design Decision: A visual workflow status bar was introduced at the top of the patient page to represent each stage of the operational journey.
Why: Displaying progress visually allows users to instantly recognize patient status without searching through records, reducing cognitive effort and improving workflow awareness.

2. Communicating Urgency Through Color Coding
Problem: Users often missed deadlines or follow-ups because important dates were buried within text-based information.
Design Decision: Color-coded indicators were added to workflow milestones:
  • Red for due or overdue dates
  • Yellow for upcoming dates
  • Green for successfully completed stages
Why: Color enables rapid recognition of urgency and status without requiring users to read detailed information, supporting quick decision-making in fast-paced clinical environments.

3. Supporting Proactive Task Management
Problem: Staff workflows were reactive rather than proactive, causing delays in insurance claims and patient processing.
Design Decision: Upcoming milestones were highlighted using yellow indicators to signal approaching tasks before they become critical.
Why: Early visual reminders help staff prepare in advance, reducing last-minute actions and improving operational efficiency.

4. Reducing Errors and Missed Steps
Problem: Without a clear process overview, steps in billing or authorization were sometimes skipped.
Design Decision: The status bar follows a linear progression aligned with real clinic workflows (New → Pending → Scheduled → Billed → Pending Payment → Completed)
Why: Mapping the interface to real-world processes reinforces user mental models and ensures tasks are completed in the correct order.

5. Providing Clear Completion Feedback
Problem: Users frequently double-checked completed tasks due to uncertainty about completion status.
Design Decision: Completed stages are marked with green indicators showing successful progress.
Why: Clear completion feedback builds user confidence and reduces unnecessary verification work.

Design Decisions

1. Providing a Clear Operational Overview
Problem: Administrative staff lacked a quick way to understand clinic performance and daily priorities because information was scattered across calendars, notes, and manual tracking systems.
Design Decision: A centralized dashboard was designed to present key operational metrics, financial summaries, and workflow updates in one unified view.
Why: Giving users an at a glance overview helps them quickly understand clinic status, prioritize tasks, and start their day without navigating through multiple sections.

2. Highlighting Critical Business Metrics
Problem: Important financial and operational indicators such as outstanding balances and cancellations were difficult to monitor consistently.
Design Decision: High priority metrics were displayed using prominent summary cards, including outstanding balance, cancellations, and revenue insights.
Why: Visual emphasis ensures users immediately notice critical information that requires action, supporting faster operational decisions.

3. Supporting Data-Driven Decision Making
Problem: Staff and managers had limited visibility into performance trends and service outcomes.
Design Decision: Analytics components such as revenue charts, insurance analytics, and sales summaries were integrated into the dashboard.
Why: Visual data representations allow users to identify trends, compare performance, and make informed decisions without needing complex reports.

4. Prioritizing Daily Workflow Tasks
Problem: Users needed quick access to patients requiring attention without manually checking schedules.
Design Decision: A “Pending Scheduled” section was introduced to display patients awaiting action, along with status and insurance details.
Why: Surfacing actionable items directly on the dashboard reduces task discovery time and helps staff focus on immediate responsibilities.

5. Improving Financial Transparency
Problem: Tracking payments and transactions required switching between systems, increasing administrative effort.
Design Decision: A real time transactions panel was added to show recent payments, refunds, and financial activity.
Why: Providing instant financial visibility improves awareness and allows staff to quickly verify payment activity.

6. Designing for Scanability and Low Cognitive Load
Problem: Complex ERP dashboards can overwhelm users with excessive information.
Design Decision: Information was organized using modular cards, clear spacing, and visual hierarchy to separate metrics, analytics, and task-based content.
Why: Information was organized using modular cards, clear spacing, and visual hierarchy to separate metrics, analytics, and task-based content.

7. Enabling Quick Navigation and Actions
Problem: Users needed fast access to commonly used actions such as searching records, viewing calendars, and generating reports.
Design Decision: Primary actions were placed prominently at the top of the dashboard with clear call-to-action buttons.
Why: Reducing navigation steps improves workflow efficiency and encourages frequent system use.

deliver.text:
The ERP system was delivered through a structured, user-centered design process focused on real clinic workflows and measurable impact.

Validation & Refinement

Design decisions were continuously validated against user needs and workflow efficiency goals. Feedback helped refine navigation, status tracking, and dashboard prioritization.

Final Delivery

The final ERP system centralized patient data, streamlined insurance tracking, and introduced visual workflow management. The solution reduced onboarding time, minimized staff dependency, and significantly improved operational efficiency.

onboarding.title: Designing LSE CRM around Real Users

overview.text: Lasenda, an accounting service company, faced major operational inefficiencies due to limitations of their existing CRM, Hawksoft. The system lacked essential task-tracking capabilities, making it difficult to monitor employee progress and manage workloads. Weak data encryption posed security concerns for sensitive financial information. additionally, Hawksoft provided no reliable method for handling client deadlines, increasing the risk of delays and compliance issues.

onboarding.problem: "Outdated CRM causes major inefficiency, security risks, and missed deadlines."

goal.title: Transforming workflow through secure, tailored software.
goal.text:
• Develop a secure, centralized system tailored to Lasenda's workflow.
  • Enable clear tracking of employee tasks, workloads and project progress.
  • Implement stronger data protection and encryption measures for financial information.
  • introduced automated, reliable client-deadline management to reduce missed submission.
  • Create a flexible develipment process that adapts to evolving stakeholder needs.

discover.text: To gain a deep understanding of Lasenda's operational challenges and user needs, a 5 day interview based research phase was conducted with key stakeholders and end users. These sessions focused on uncovering daily workflows, identifying pain points within the existing Hawksoft system, and understanding unmet requirements related to task management, data security and deadline handling. Insights gathered from these interviews directly informed the product requirements and helped prioritized features that would deliver the greatest impact in the LSE system.

define.text:
Background
Lasenda, an accounting services company, was experiencing operational inefficiencies due to limitations in their existing CRM system. After conducting stakeholder interviews (Super Admin, Admin, Supervisor, and Employees), I created a journey map to visualize the current workflow and uncover pain points across roles.The journey map captures the end-to-end process from client onboarding to task completion, highlighting breakdowns in task tracking, deadline management, and data security.

Key User Roles Identified

  • Customer – New or existing client 
  • Super Admin – Manages onboarding and system-level actions
  • Admin – Handles profile creation and account setup
  • Supervisor – Assigns and monitors tasks
  • Employee – Executes accounting tasks

Client Onboarding - Pain Points
  • Manual data entry
  • No structured onboarding flow
  • Difficult to manage multiple account types
  • Risk of incomplete or inconsistent information

Assign to Supervisor - Pain Points
  • No clear visibility of assignment history
  • Difficult to track supervisor workload
  • Limited progress transparency

Assign to Staff Member - Pain Points
  • Cannot assign tasks to multiple departments efficiently
  • No real-time task tracking
  • Hard to monitor progress
  • No automated notifications for new assignments

Task Completion - Pain Points
  • No structured deadline management
  • No automated reminders
  • Limited performance monitoring
  • Risk of delayed compliance submissions

Insights:

There is no centralized way to track task status, employee workload, or assignment flow. This reduces accountability and transparency.The absence of automated deadline tracking increases the risk of delays and compliance issues.Weak encryption mechanisms create risks when handling sensitive financial data.The workflow depends heavily on manual coordination between roles, increasing operational friction.

 Opportunity Areas:
  • Introduce structured onboarding forms
  • Enable task progress tracking dashboards
  • Add deadline management with automated notifications
  • Support multi-department assignment
  • Implement stronger data encryption
  • Auto-generate client IDs and agreement documents
  • Centralize relevant regulatory links

design.intro:
After clearly defining the core problems during the Define phase,  including poor task visibility, weak deadline management, and security concerns, I transitioned into the Design phase with a focused objective:To create a structured, secure, and transparent CRM experience that improves workflow efficiency across all roles. 

During this phase, I focused on:

  • Designing a clearer task assignment and tracking system
  • Improving deadline visibility with automated notifications
  • Creating structured onboarding flows
  • Strengthening data handling touch points
  • Enhancing role based dashboards for better transparency

items.text:
Problem: Users don’t know what’s pending, what’s ongoing, or what’s completed. Users struggle to identify what needs urgent attention.Updates and conversations are spread across emails, chats, and calls.Users don’t know who is responsible for what.
Solution:
  • Kanban Layout (Todo | In Progress | Completed)
  • Clear Task count indicators
  • Visual status separation using color coded sections
  • Priority Tags
  • Strong visual contrast for deadlines
  • Structured card with summaries
  • assignee avatars visible on each task
  • Centralized task based collaboration
  • Sort by newest
  • Filter by client, employee, department
  • Inline Task creation

Overall UX Impact

  • Reduces mental load
  • Improves clarity and accountability
  • Centralizes communication
  • Makes prioritization visual
  • Enables faster decision-making
Transformed task management from reactive chaos to structured, visual workflow control.

Problem:
Client onboarding often involves multiple departments, billing rules, fees, and documents , which can overwhelm users. Too many inputs on one screen can cause confusion and mistakes. Financial fields are often unclear and prone to entry errors. Uploading contracts or attachments can feel clunky. Clients may have multiple services or departments. Users worry about losing progress in long forms.
Solution:
  • Step-based vertical progress navigation (Business Info → Department Info → Payment Info → etc.)
  • Clear step indicators with numbering
  • Logical grouping of related fields
  • Section-based grouping (Department Info, Billing, Location)
  • Currency selector beside each amount
  • Payment method clearly selectable
  • Visible uploaded file confirmation
  • Modular department configuration

Overall UX Impact

  • Breaks down complexity into structured steps
  • Reduces billing errors
  • Supports scalable client setups
  • Improve data clarity
Transformed a traditionally overwhelming client setup into a guided, modular, and error-resistant experience.

Problem:
The existing invoicing system was inefficient, manual, and lacked visibility. Users struggled with inconsistent invoice creation, manual calculations, and poor payment status tracking. There was no structured workflow, no automated reminders for due dates, and limited transparency into outstanding payments.
Solution:
  • A guided, step-by-step invoice creation process was introduced to reduce errors and ensure complete data entry.
  • The system now auto-calculates totals, taxes, and service fees based on predefined rules.
  • Invoices now display real-time status indicators (Draft, Sent, Overdue, Paid).
  • Payment due dates are clearly highlighted, with automated reminders.
  • A dashboard view allows filtering by client, status, and date.

Overall UX Impact

  • Efficiency (less time spent creating and tracking invoices)
  • Accuracy (reduced billing errors)
  • Visibility (clear payment tracking)
  • Accountability (defined ownership and status clarity)
Ultimately, the redesign strengthened operational reliability while improving the overall user experience for Admins and Supervisors.

deliver.text:
After completing the Design phase, the finalized UI designs and prototypes were handed over to the development team to begin implementation. The handoff included detailed design specifications, user flows, and interaction guidelines to ensure accurate translation of design decisions into the final product. However, the process did not end at handoff. Since the project requirements evolved alongside business needs, continuous collaboration became a key part of the workflow.

Weekly Client Collaboration: Throughout development, weekly meetings were conducted with stakeholders and clients to:

  • Clarify design requirements
  • Address implementation questions
  • Validate workflows against real business processes
  • Capture requirement changes and newly identified needs
These sessions ensured alignment between design, development, and business expectations.

UX Role During Development: During this stage, my role shifted from designer to UX collaborator and design validator, where I:
  • Explained design decisions to developers
  • Updated designs based on new requirements
  • Refined user flows when business processes changed
  • Ensured usability was maintained despite scope adjustments
  • Prevented deviations from the intended user experience

Impact on the Product: Continuous UX involvement during development helped:
  • Reduce misunderstandings between stakeholders and developers
  • Adapt the system to evolving client needs
  • Maintain design consistency throughout implementation
  • Minimize rework by validating decisions early
This iterative collaboration ensured that the final product remained user-centered while accommodating real-world operational changes.
